issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a male torture survivor, sexual-trauma-specific verbal cues are possible only if sexual torture or sexual humiliation is part of the trauma, but the rest of the profile provides no corresponding sexual content in memory, appraisals, threat, or coping. As selected, this trigger appears disconnected from the trauma representation and is hard to justify clinically.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The appraisal that others can visibly see what happened to him implies shame/marked visible contamination or exposure. That could occur after torture, but here it is not supported by the memory items, trigger content, or other appraisals, making it feel mismatched with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: Gambling as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is poorly linked to the active formulation. The main connected pattern is triggers ↔ negative appraisals with memory-linked re-experiencing and threat-driven compliance/detachment. Gambling introduces a separate excitement-seeking coping style that is not reflected elsewhere and feels clinically disconnected rather than integrated.

vignette:
Carlos was seventy, a welder who had spent forty years in the United States after fleeing torture in El Salvador. In his early twenties he had been a union organizer; paramilitaries abducted him from his home, blindfolded him, and held him for three days in a windowless cell. They beat him with rifle butts, put a pistol to his head and pulled the trigger on an empty chamber, and fired live rounds into the wall beside him. He could do nothing-his hands were bound, his mouth taped, and every noise told him he was utterly without options. The worst part, he later told himself, was that he had not fought back; he had gone limp, nodded when they demanded information he did not have. He was released, eventually, but the shame and the fury stayed.

In the decades that followed, Carlos built a quiet life-raised a daughter, worked long shifts in fabrication shops. But the triggers were everywhere. A car backfiring outside the shop would send the gunshot noise crashing through him, and the memory would arrive not as a recollection but as a present-tense assault: he could taste the grime of the blindfold, feel the cold concrete against his back, and the rage would surge so hot that his hands shook. And in that moment the conviction solidified: this is what he got for not fighting back-he had only himself to blame. When he tried to explain what had happened to a coworker, he would lose the thread mid-sentence and stop, the words dissolving into a jumble of images he could not sequence. That inability to describe it cleanly only deepened another conviction: the event had happened because of the way he had acted-because he had been passive, compliant-and he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop it.

His work routine became a minefield. Narrow welding booths, with their enclosed sides and limited exits, triggered the sensation of entrapment: having no options, just like in that cell. The feeling of being cornered would instantly revive the memory's presence, and with it the gnawing fear that he could never know who would harm him next-any stranger, any coworker, any sudden noise could be a threat. To cope, Carlos developed habits that were barely conscious. When a trigger struck, he would force himself to suppress the thoughts, trying to push the images away. At the same time, he would detach from the memory, watching himself as if from a distance, numb. And when he felt threatened-say, a foreman raised his voice-Carlos would become overly compliant, nodding, agreeing, offering no resistance, the same posture he had taken in the torture chamber. The guilt he carried made this fawn response automatic: he believed that if he had acted differently then, he would not have suffered, so now he tried to preempt any danger by placating. That same guilt taught him to see danger in ordinary exchanges-a raised voice in the next bay, a sudden step behind him-so that anything unexpected could become a signal that he was about to fail again.

The hypervigilance that grew from his fear of harm turned every unexpected noise into a potential trigger, and the memory itself-so raw, so present-functioned as its own trigger, sending him into a spiral of scanning and vigilance. Over the months he began avoiding any situation that felt enclosed or unpredictable. He turned down welding jobs in tight crawl spaces. He left a grocery store once because a child's balloon popped. At home he would sit in his armchair with the television off, trying to stay inside a bare, quiet room where no surprises could reach him.

His daughter finally insisted he see someone after he froze for ten minutes at the sound of a dropped steel beam, unable to speak or move, the memory so vivid he had not known where he was. Carlos came to the clinic afraid that his mind was broken, but also hoping-desperately, silently-that there might be a way to stop the cycle without having to stay numb forever.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not show that triggers (e.g., backfiring cars, narrow booths) directly cause negative appraisals (self-blame, guilt). The negative appraisals are presented as stable beliefs, not activated by triggers.
The vignette does not show that negative appraisals lead to triggers. Instead, hypervigilance (stemming from fear of harm) turns noises into triggers, not the self-blame itself.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not show that triggers (e.g., backfiring cars, narrow booths) directly cause negative appraisals (self-blame, guilt). The negative appraisals are presented as stable beliefs, not activated by triggers.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals lead to triggers. Instead, hypervigilance (stemming from fear of harm) turns noises into triggers, not the self-blame itself.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
